chunks: Ibn Mahbub narrated from Abu Muhammad al-Wabishi, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah عليه السلام about a group of people who claimed against a slave an offense encompassing his neck, and the slave confessed to it. He said: “The confession of a slave is not valid against his master.”
He said: “If they establish the evidence for what they claimed against the slave, they may take the slave for it, or his master may ransom him.”

key_terms.إِقْرَارُ الْعَبْدِ: The legal confession or admission made by the slave.
key_terms.الْبَيِّنَةَ: Legally recognized proof or evidentiary testimony.
key_terms.تُحِيطُ بِرَقَبَتِهِ: An expression indicating a grave offense exposing the slave to capital or total penal liability.
key_terms.جِنَايَةً: A criminal offense or injury entailing legal liability.
key_terms.يَفْتَدِيَهُ مَوْلَاهُ: That his master compensates or ransoms him instead of surrendering him.

ai.seo_question: Is a slave’s confession legally valid against his master in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: This hadith gives a legal ruling concerning a slave accused of a grave offense. It states that the slave’s own confession does not establish liability against his master, but a valid claim supported by evidence may allow the claimants to take the slave or for the master to ransom him.

en.bab-ul-qaim-publications:
Hadith.5270 - Ibn Mahbub narrated from Abu Muhammad Al-Wabishi who said:
I asked Abu Abdullah (as) about a group of people who claimed that a slave had committed an offense warranting his execution, and the slave confessed to it.
Imam (as) said: "The confession of a slave is not valid against his master."
Imam (as) further said: "But if they establish evidence for what they claimed against the slave, they may take the slave for it or his master may ransom him."
